headline: Six panels, six independent lenses, one verdict: AIGate is not too technical because of what it says — it is too technical because of where and how it says it. Nothing in the engine, the rules, the audit trail, or the honesty markers needs to change. What needs to change is the order, grouping and vocabulary on the four screens that never received the treatment the graph-review screen got in Round 9 — the verdict/sign-off page, the guided intake form, the register list and the appetite-framework screen — plus one screen none of the panels caught: the Confirm & attest step still shows raw codes ("traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute") at the exact moment a submitter signs their name to the description. I recommend a targeted redesign delivered as one coordinated round of five build chunks, in the R9 manner (aggregate, prioritise, put one click away — never delete). Not a copy patch: it would leave the verdict page and the form as confusing as today. Not a full redesign: no panel found a fault in the flow or the information architecture, and a rebuild would put the caveats that make the product defensible first in line to be lost. Every disagreement between panels is settled below by a stated principle rather than a vote, and every overruled position is recorded. Three facts from the code that neither round of the panels had: the sign-off buttons are already hidden from the 1LoD role today (so the role-gating fight was about a decision already shipped — the fix is to label the role switcher honestly), the verdict page already has an accessible fold component with an honesty-floor override (so the recomposition is cheaper than the panels assumed), and the "describe in plain language" path is already the default entry point.

options.name: Option A — Patch the copy
options.what: STAGE_LABELS for the register; strip internal requirement codes (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, VD-4, UC-*) from every sentence; technical terms on form options become a small muted suffix; 'firm rules (invariants)'; reword the no-basis badge; plain labels on the Confirm & attest screen; relabel the role switcher as a view preference.
options.cost: 1–2 build chunks, roughly two days of pipeline work at the project's R9/R14 pace; one or two releases; modest test churn (scoped queries, reserved-word checks).
options.risk: Low technical risk, high product risk: the verdict/sign-off page stays a wall and the intake form stays a flat list of 16 questions, so the 'too confusing' complaint survives on the two screens that matter most. This is the floor, not the fix.

options.name: Option B — Targeted redesign, one coordinated round (recommended)
options.what: Everything in A plus: verdict/sign-off page recomposed (provisional banner first, 'Before you sign off' checklist with jump links, one line per rule with all citations visible, controls as summary-then-detail, section nav, advisory qualifier at first mention); guided form grouped into five plain-language sections with help behind 'Why we ask' and no field hidden; register with a 2LoD 'awaiting your sign-off' default, grouped filters, an always-visible legend, a provisional banner and a Flags column; appetite-framework screen with the readable rulebook by default and the YAML editor behind a disclosure; graph-review label reuse, badge reword, 'not stated' flag and aria state; queue copy and source tags; header fidelity chip. Shipped as a requirements round with test cases so 'never delete' is test-enforced.
options.cost: Five build chunks in order (register → verdict → form + confirm → policy + header → graph review + queue), roughly 6–9 working days at the project's recent pace; each chunk carries the house ritual (tests ×3, typecheck, build, spec .md + .html parity, live walkthrough, commit and push). Expect to update scoped test queries in several files and to write an R-next requirements document first.
options.risk: Moderate and known: reserved-word collisions (gated per label), an implementer conflating regulatory citations with spec IDs (gated by the three-class rule), spec drift between .md and .html (parity check), and the Low-tier stage-label semantics needing a builder check before landing. No engine, audit or honesty change, so the determinism and honesty test suites remain the safety net.

options.name: Option C — Full redesign
options.what: New information architecture and visual language from a fresh mockup; re-derive every screen and every disclosure.
options.cost: 3–6 weeks plus full re-verification of ~540 tests; discards field-copy.ts, the R9 and R14 recompositions and the accessible fold infrastructure that already work where applied.
options.risk: Highest. The hedged-sounding caveats that make the product defensible — 'self-asserted, not verified', 'restates the record; it does not strengthen it', 'proof-of-concept grade' — are the first casualties of a 'make it feel finished' pass; and no panel found a fault in the flow or architecture that would justify it. Not recommended.

The proposal's core recommendation is sound and unusually well-grounded in the actual source — every claim I spot-checked against GraphView.tsx, ConfirmationStep.tsx, RegisterDetail.tsx, register.ts and field-copy.ts held up, including the two novel code-level facts (role gating already shipped; UC-6 raw codes at attestation). But the fix for that very raw-code defect is scoped to the wrong surface: the same graphSummaryRows() function that produces "traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute" also renders inside VerdictDisplay.tsx's Record & provenance panel on the verdict/sign-off page — the exact page §3.1 is redesigning for Priya — and no part of §3.1 or §3.5 names or fixes that second call site, so a 2LoD reviewer would still meet raw codes at sign-off after the round ships. Separately, the new "Before you sign off" checklist plus a sticky nav item that jumps straight to Sign-off lets a reviewer reach Approve in one click without ever touching the reasoning or evidence — reintroducing, under a different name, the exact ritual-checking risk the chair explicitly rejected ID-4's sticky Approve bar for — and the audit trail's actor field is the same self-asserted, ungated role string that drives whether the Approve button even renders, yet only the signer's name gets an honesty caveat, not the role. Recommend: fix the graph-summary scope gap and the nav/checklist rubber-stamp path before the R-next ticket is written; both are small, targeted amendments that don't touch the recommendation itself.

The core call — targeted redesign, presentation-only, five chunks in the R9 manner — is sound and every constraint that matters (engine island, determinism, append-only audit, honesty markers) is genuinely respected; most of the chair's "facts from the code" check out under direct inspection. But the headline claim that the verdict/sign-off page "never received the Round-9 treatment" is factually wrong — requirements-014.md shows an R14 recomposition applying that exact idiom (folds, honesty-floor-never-folds, "What you need to do" moved under the headline) was approved and shipped in the same v0.16.0 build the chair reviewed, which both inflates chunk 2's portrayed scope/cost and undercuts the document's central "we found what the panels couldn't see" claim. Five further concrete gaps — a shared raw-code-rendering function split across two build chunks, a checklist that visually promises interactivity it doesn't have, a register column change that contradicts an existing Must-level test/spec requirement without a planned requirements amendment, an under-flagged collision with the codebase's known brittle `/approved|rejected/i` test pattern on the exact page being rewritten, and one internally contradictory build gate — need fixing before a build session should start, but none of them touch the recommendation itself: this survives as Option B once those six items are corrected in the document.
